data.title: Smithing and iron currency bars in antiquity and in the Slavic period
data.excerpt: From their arrival in the territory of present-day Slovakia in about the 5th century until the 11th century the Slavs knew coins, but neither minted nor used them as a standard currency. Their recognised currency, the direct forerunner of money here, was the axe-shaped currency bar. The article looks at the working of iron from antiquity to the Middle Ages and at the commonest types of bar.
data.metaTitle: Smithing and iron currency bars in the Slavic period
data.metaDescription: The Slavs minted no coins of their own, yet they did have a currency — iron bars. A look at smithing and iron metallurgy from antiquity to the Slavic period.

children.text: In the period from their arrival in the territory of present-day Slovakia sometime in the 5th century until the 11th century the Slavs did know coins, since they encountered them both in trade contacts with Byzantium and on various military campaigns, but they neither produced nor used them as a standard currency. That does not mean, however, that our Slavic ancestors used no generally exchangeable currency of their own. Besides precious metals, furs and linen, in the time of Great Moravia merchants used as currency something that could be described as a kind of first currency of the Slavs. This recognised currency, the direct forerunner of money in the territory of present-day Slovakia, was the
axe-shaped currency bar.
In this article, taken for the most part from the website of the
archaeology students
, we bring you, with the authors' consent, a short look at the working of iron in antiquity and the Middle Ages and at the development and the most frequently used types of currency bar.

children.text: The beginnings of iron production and tradable raw materials

The beginning of iron production was preceded by the established production and working of copper and its alloys, which in Europe has its roots as far back as the close of the Eneolithic. Even earlier than that, however, as early as the 7th to 5th millennia BC, some tribes in the Near East had mastered this technology. During the Bronze Age the exhaustion of the deposits known until then began to make itself felt, which was one of the reasons why people began to look around for another metal that would satisfy the ever-growing demand. On the basis of very isolated finds it may be assumed that the first human encounter with metallic iron took place long before 3000 BC in the territory of the eastern Mediterranean. At first this was mainly meteoritic iron (characterised by a high nickel content), or iron produced by chance. In the third and second millennia BC the first iron-smelting furnaces began to operate in the Near East and in Anatolia, producing above all weapons and objects of exceptional importance. The emergence of iron smelting is closely linked to the established technology of copper production, in which the smelting of sulphide ore produces iron as a by-product, a waste product. The two technologies separated towards the end of the 2nd millennium BC, but this still concerns only the area of the eastern Mediterranean. The question of where iron metallurgy originated is still unanswered. Knowledge of iron production reached Europe through the Mediterranean, Macedonia, northern Serbia and into the eastern foothills of the Alps, from where it then spread freely to the other parts of Central and Northern Europe. Knowledge of ironworking reached Central Europe only in the Hallstatt period, around the 8th century BC.

In Central Europe, and thus also in the territory of present-day Slovakia, specialised villages arose in the 8th–9th centuries AD directly in the vicinity of the iron ore deposits. In these villages we have evidence not only of furnaces for working iron, but also of associated activities such as charcoal burning. One example is the area of the Moravian Karst, where ironworking is attested as early as the 6th century BC. The smithy in the Býčí skála cave dates from this period. In the Iron Age iron ore was obtained only by collecting surface occurrences, but in time the area was picked clean. From the Slavic period (that is, from the 7th to the 11th century) come archaeological finds of old smelting works around Rudice, Olomučany and Habrůvka. Iron ore was still obtained by collection, but extraction in shallow mine workings begins to spread.

Intensive mining of iron ore in the territory of Moravia took place as early as the 8th century, when the deposits in the settled areas, above all in southern Moravia, had been exhausted and other sources had to be found. In addition, this area had dense forests which provided good-quality wood for charcoal burning. This was another raw material needed for the production of iron which was lacking in the already inhabited areas. Another undoubted advantage of the Moravian Karst was the proximity of the wealthy hillforts in southern Moravia, where most of the iron ultimately went.
 
From this example we can therefore see that
the working of iron
compared, for instance, with the working of gold
was far more demanding.

Whereas gold only needed to be melted down and cast, iron demanded a procedure that could take several days of intensive work. Unlike gold, however, a relatively large quantity of malleable iron mass was produced, which allowed it to be used even for bulkier objects and for objects of everyday use. Perhaps it was these very properties that led people to sense its potential as a tradable commodity, and later
iron in various forms also took on the role of a pre-coinage currency
. For iron to turn from a material into a tradable commodity or a currency, it had to be worked into some agreed form,
and so the currency bar came into being
, an object typified by its elongated shape, flattened at one end.
In the hands of a smith it could then be transformed into other objects

that were made of iron, for example fittings, harness, agricultural tools and weapons. Metallographic analyses have refuted the old claim that the bar itself could have been a tool, for instance a carpenter's axe, or a weapon. The analyses showed that the flattened part had not been metallurgically improved in any way, and so was not intended for working harder materials.
Iron currency bars in the territory of present-day Slovakia

In the Late Hallstatt period iron was mostly imported into Central and Eastern Europe, but the beginning of small-scale production at the settlements there is also reckoned with. Traces of this production are known, for instance, from Poland, but also from the territory of present-day Slovakia.

In these places, besides iron currency bars, other related objects of a similar purpose were also produced. These are iron blooms. A bloom is smelted iron worked into a simple rounded flat shape resembling a cake or a loaf (hence the name loaf-shaped bloom). Its functions were very similar, but unlike the bars they were always made of fresh raw material. In the case of the bars, examination has shown that the material was often recycled, probably therefore from broken or otherwise unusable objects. This fact further underlines the value of iron: nothing went to waste. Blooms were highly valued right up to the Middle Ages, and by a lucky chance several examples have survived. Finds of them are so far known from Slovakia; in the Czech lands they are still lacking.

children.text: A large bloom with two unusually large axes was found in Slovakia in a Hallstatt settlement feature in front of the Fajka cave near Jasov. It is a bulky piece of metal with black corrosion, of irregular shape and with a lumpy surface. The base formed under its own weight while the raw material was still doughy; the weight of the piece is about 2 kg. Further Hallstatt blooms have survived at Krásna Hôrka in the village of Medvedzie in the Orava region. Among the iron and bronze objects there were also three pieces of iron semi-finished products. Their shape is slightly prismatic, which points to more thorough forging and deliberate shaping into some form. The maker probably prepared their shape in advance for further forming. From the turn of the Hallstatt and La Tène periods, double-pointed bars with a bent point, half a bar with bronze rings rusted onto it, and bars with holes and bent points have survived at Býčí skála. A parallel is to be sought as far away as Old Assyria, where whole stores of these bars have been discovered.

blocks.alt: Smithing and iron currency bars in antiquity and in the Slavic period

children.text: Hoards of axe-shaped currency bars already from the Great Moravian period come from
Bíňa, Pobedim and Bojná
, and most recently, for example, from
Pružina

. These hoards were found within the enclosure of a hillfort. Hoards from Gajary-pustiny, Vrablicovo and Kúty then come from settlement layers. For some hoards it is possible to establish a relationship to a specific structural feature, as is the case precisely at Pobedim, where we have evidence of two hoards, one of which was deposited in a sunken settlement feature and the other beneath the collapse of the rampart.

Most hoards in general, however, are in a natural setting without traces of human intervention. In some cases, though, it can be supposed that they lay in an artificially made container, which may be indicated by a suspicious accumulation of stones around them, for example the hoard from Slabina, which was covered by a large stone, or that at Moravský Ján. At Staré Město a quernstone served instead of a flat stone.
From Mikulčice comes an assemblage of objects that was probably wrapped in linen, as is suggested by the impressions of fibres.

blocks.caption: Top left, axe-shaped currency bars from the Pružina hillfort (9th–10th century)
blocks.alt: Top left, axe-shaped currency bars from the Pružina hillfort (9th–10th century)

children.text: When we turn to analysing the contents of the hoards, we arrive at interesting insights. Hoards containing only axe-shaped currency bars (Bíňa and Pobedim, mentioned above), or axe-shaped bars together with other iron objects, are concentrated mainly at hillforts, either in settlement features or in places within the enclosure where no fighting took place. This suggests that they are above all hoarded (concealed) property. Hoards containing only axe-shaped bars may represent currency or raw material intended for further working. In my view, if the bars are found in connection with a smithy, it is appropriate to regard them as the raw material from which the smith made iron objects. In other cases they may be either a merchant's concealed currency or the concealed property of a wealthier person.
Another rich hoard, of forty iron currency bars, comes from
Hrádok

(Nové Mesto nad Váhom). The bars were deposited in bundles of twenty; the total weight of the hoard is about 65 kg.
Other find spots of axe-shaped currency bars: Staré zámky u Líšně, Nejdek, Mikulčice, Břeclav-Pohansko.

children.text: The variety of shapes of iron currency bars and semi-finished products
Double-pointed bars

Double-pointed bars date from the Hallstatt period. They have the shape of a double-pointed pyramid, with bent and often pierced ends. In the La Tène period this type persists, but now with straight ends. Often only parts or fragments of bars are found, which can look like small chisels; a heavily corroded object in particular can easily be confused with them.
This type of bar tends to be associated with the Celts, because the greatest concentration of finds comes from the areas where their original homeland would be sought.
Loaf-shaped blooms

Blooms were worked differently in technological terms. They were not forged, which can be seen both on the surface and on a broken or split piece, because there are bubbles inside. They were made of fresh iron which, white-hot, was poured into a soft mould or onto a slab, where it solidified and took its shape. The iron could also be poured into water, where it cooled very rapidly and the shape was very irregular and jagged, and the whole structure is spongy.

blocks.alt: Smithing and iron currency bars in antiquity and in the Slavic period

children.text:
Loaf-shaped blooms were split with an axe while still glowing hot, in order to establish the success of the smelt and the quality of the material. This custom is known throughout Northern and Eastern Europe (Russia, Poland, Norway, Sweden, Lithuania). For this shape of bloom the term horseshoe-shaped is sometimes used.
The weight of Old Russian blooms ranges from 2 to 6 kg.
Axe-shaped currency bars

This kind of bar was originally regarded as a tool (an adze, for working clay, a quernstone), but their edge is too thin. The eye for the haft is of normal size, but sometimes the object is provided with butt lugs. Because of corrosion and other adverse influences it is very difficult to determine their original weight precisely. The weight of the bars was not random. Examination of the bars found allows them to be divided by weight into three groups: 200–700 g, 80–120 g and 60–80 g. In the time of Great Moravia it was precisely axe-shaped bars that were used as a generally accepted currency, which we therefore rightly regard as the forerunner of money in the territory of present-day Slovakia. Their use is recorded in the course of the 9th and 10th centuries mainly in the territory of Slovakia, Bohemia and Moravia.
Disc

Similar in shape to a bloom, but this is already a forged form. It is not entirely common; it is possible that the smith who made this semi-finished product already had in mind some further working into an object based on a circle. An exceptional find from Kolčina.
Rod, bar

This form of currency bar is the commonest in the Middle Ages. It developed from the axe-shaped bar, which began to lose its specific features such as the (cross-wise) flattening, the eyes and so on. Although the loss of the eyes deprived this object of easy portability, it was more practical for working and for measuring out. Often only the piece that was needed for production was struck off the bars, and it was easy to measure out.
The production of currency bars and iron-working technologies

Like us, the old smiths were familiar with the concepts of iron and steel, and it did not take long before they understood how to produce good-quality steel and exploit its properties. Probably when changing the fuel used in working iron they realised how some fuels could affect the hardness of the material, and they began to prefer fuels capable of supplying the iron with carbon. Of course, at that time the smiths had to distinguish these differences without any knowledge of chemistry and physics. Most often we can recognise the quality of the metal by making it ring with a blow or by a file test: when passing over soft metal the file bites, on hard steel it does not.

Iron today corresponds to the soft kinds of steel, which cannot be hardened and contain about 0.06–0.2% C, and which are used to make various fittings, cramps, hooks, hoops or couplings. Carbon steels, by contrast, are suitable for tools, because they can be hardened. They serve as material for making scythes, sickles, knives, chisels and shears. Yet another type are alloy (alloyed) tool steels, which contain a significant proportion of further elements, for example manganese or chromium. It must be mentioned that every steel contains an admixture of some element, though in a very small quantity; nevertheless even a small quantity can determine its properties.
Carbon substantially increases hardness and strength, but also brittleness and cold-shortness, and makes welding more difficult. Manganese gives the material strength, hardness, malleability and weldability, while reducing ductility and toughness. With a higher manganese content (2–4%) overheating of the material and coarsening of the structure can occur. Silicon is present only modestly in old finds (0.02–0.04%), but phosphorus could greatly affect the quality of the material under the conditions of historical production. At lower temperatures most of it usually passed into the slag, but the element captured by the metal markedly affected the hardness of the alloy and also its castability, cold-shortness and cold brittleness. Phosphorus is wholly unsuitable for the production of steel, because it also affects the other processes in its manufacture in undesirable ways. There should be no more than 0.1% phosphorus in steel; in high-grade materials only 0.04–0.07% is permissible. In prehistory it was customary to use charcoal for the production of iron, and so its sulphur content is not very high. In iron that was worked over coke, by contrast, we find considerably more sulphur. It causes brittleness and hot-shortness and is regarded as a very harmful element. Copper is a very common admixture in iron and is not undesirable; it improves strength and resistance to corrosion. Nickel is also a common admixture. If the nickel content in iron is higher than 2.5%, it can only be iron of meteoritic origin.
In talents and in iron blooms we find the elements mentioned, which entered them through working. In the case of iron currency bars it is possible that some element will be present in a conspicuously higher proportion. This may be recycled iron, an object which had been carburised, for example, for better properties, but which broke or wore out and was reworked back into a bar so as to be given a new form. The production of bars was more complicated than the production of blooms. The first step, common to almost all types, was to work the material into a long bar. This was followed by forging out into various forms. Probably the most interesting is the making of an axe-shaped bar, where one end was flattened out more and extended over roughly two thirds of the bar. The other end was also flattened, but transversely to the first, and an eye was marked out in it, which served for tying several pieces together, making transport easier. Punching is the quickest way of providing iron objects with a hole and is done while they are glowing hot. Compared with drilling it has the advantage of respecting the grain of the material and stretching it. This makes it possible to pierce even large holes in narrow strips. Punching is carried out over a round hole in the anvil using a punch of hard steel and a hammer. The hole is driven in to about two thirds, then the object is turned over and the driving is repeated from the other side.
